body.statement: For every \(k\ge0\) and \(n\ge2k+4\), \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) and therefore \[D_k(n)=2^{k+1}.\] One original coefficient \(e^{\star}\) separates all branches on a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(d=k+1\) and \(N=2d+2=2k+4\).  We first treat the graph on exactly \(N\) vertices.  In the graph of \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), the directed edges are
\[
 0\to P_i,\qquad 0\to Q_i,\qquad P_i\to h
 \quad(1\leq i\leq d).
\]
The supplied arborescence consists of the first \(2d\) edges and \(P_1\to h\).  Hence
\[
 |T|=2d+1=N-1,\qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\leq i\leq d\},\qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Every nonroot vertex has exactly one incoming edge in \(T\), every vertex is reached from \(0\), and
\[
 0,P_1,Q_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_d,h
\]
is a topological order.  Thus the acyclicity and arborescence conditions in \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\) hold, and (1) proves
\[
 (G^{\star}_{k,N},T,e^{\star})\in\mathcal G_{N,k}.             \tag{2}
\]

We now construct a regular covariance fiber.  Choose positive rational numbers \(h_i\) and rational numbers \(b_i\) such that
\[
 b_i^2>4h_i\qquad(1\leq i\leq d),
\]
and set \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  Choose a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\), sufficiently close to \(H_0\), with diagonal \((h_1,\ldots,h_d)\); a further generic restriction on its off-diagonal entries will be imposed below.  In the vertex order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), define
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0&0&1\\
  0&H&H&0\\
  0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
  1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.                       \tag{3}
\]
Choose rational \(C_0\) so that \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  Since \(H\succ0\), the Schur complement of \(H\) in the \((P,Q)\)-principal block of (3) is
\[
 C_0I_d-HH^{-1}H=C_0I_d-H\succ0.
\]
Thus that principal block is positive definite.  The \(0\)-coordinate is independent of the \((P,Q)\)-block, and choosing rational \(M\) larger than the final Schur-complement threshold therefore gives
\[
 Sigma^{\star}\succ0.                                       \tag{4}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\qquad c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\qquad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\qquad z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad x=-Hz.
\]
The only absent bidirected pairs are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\), for \(1\leq i\leq d\).  Substitution of (3) into the residual formula defining \(F_{ij}\) gives, respectively,
\[
 0=h_i+a_ic_i,\qquad
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,\qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i.                                            \tag{5}
\]
Because \(H\) is positive definite and hence invertible, (5) is equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,\qquad c_i=x_i+b_i,\qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d),
 \qquad z=-H^{-1}x.                                          \tag{6}
\]
The discriminant of the \(i\)-th quadratic is \(b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Consequently (6) has exactly \(2^d\) real solutions.  Under the invertible linear change \(z\mapsto x=-Hz\), the Jacobian of the \(3d\) equations in (5), with respect to \((a,c,z)\), is nonsingular precisely when
\[
 det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.                          \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, for each \(i\), the determinant of the three corresponding equations in \((a_i,c_i,x_i)\) is, up to sign, \(a_i+c_i=2x_i+b_i\), and at a solution
\[
 (2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0.
\]
Thus all \(2^d\) solutions are reduced.  For each solution define
\[
 \Omega=(I_N-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{\star}(I_N-\Lambda). \tag{8}
\]
Equations (5) say exactly that every required missing off-diagonal entry of \(\Omega\) is zero.  The displayed topological order makes \(I_N-\Lambda\) unit triangular and therefore invertible.  Equation (4) and congruence in (8) imply \(\Omega\succ0\).  Hence every point in (6) is a real supported positive-definite source lift of the same covariance.

It remains to make the queried coordinate distinguish the \(2^d\) lifts.  At \(H=H_0\), two branches whose first coordinates differ have distinct values \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If \(x\ne x'\) have the same first coordinate, choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and put \(H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1})\).  Differentiating \(-H(s)^{-1}x\) at zero gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\{z_1(x)-z_1(x')\}\right|_{s=0}
   =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.                              \tag{9}
\]
Thus, for every pair of distinct branches, equality of their \(z_1\)-values is a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  There are finitely many pairs.  A finite union of proper algebraic subsets cannot contain a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\), and rational matrices are dense in that neighborhood.  We may therefore choose the rational positive-definite \(H\) in (3) outside this union.  For that choice the \(2^d\) values of
\[
 z_1=\lambda_{e^{\star}}
\]
are pairwise distinct.

We next pass from this regular special fiber to the generic field degree.  There are \(3d\) directed coordinates and exactly \(3d\) absent bidirected pairs.  Because every other pair is bidirected,
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left(\binom N2-3d\right)+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2=:M_0.                                      \tag{10}
\]
Perturb all \(M_0\) independent entries of \(\Sigma^{\star}\) by algebraically independent variables \(\xi\).  At any one of the reduced points \(v_0=(a,c,z)\), seek a formal solution
\[
 v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\geq1}v_r(\xi),
\]
where \(v_r\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) in \(\xi\).  After the lower-degree terms have been determined, the degree-\(r\) part of the residual equations is
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}).                      \tag{11}
\]
The matrix \(J(v_0)\) is invertible by (7), so (11) uniquely determines \(v_r\) for every \(r\).  Hence each of the \(2^d\) displayed points determines a formal section over the entire covariance formal neighborhood.

If \(f\in P_G\), then after any such section is substituted, (8) supplies a supported source lift and therefore
\[
 f(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi)=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb C[[\xi]].
\]
Translation by \(\Sigma^{\star}\) is injective on the covariance polynomial ring, because the entries of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent.  It follows that
\[
 P_G=(0),\qquad K_G=\mathbb C(\sigma_{ij}:i\leq j).            \tag{12}
\]
By (10), \(L\) and \(K_G\) have the same transcendence degree \(M_0\).  Since \(L\) is finitely generated over \(K_G\), the extension \(L/K_G\) is finite.  By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), its generic fiber is the integral residual fiber and no directed-coordinate expression has been inverted.

Partition the directed variables into singleton blocks \(A_i=(a_i)\), singleton blocks \(C_i=(c_i)\), and the size-\(d\) block \(Z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\).  From the defining formula for \(F_{ij}\), the three residual equations associated with index \(i\) have block degrees bounded respectively by
\[
 A_i+C_i,\qquad A_i+Z,\qquad C_i+Z.
\]
Because \(L/K_G\) is finite and has characteristic zero, its \([L:K_G]\) embeddings give \([L:K_G]\) distinct isolated points of the geometric generic residual fiber: the disturbance coordinates are recovered from \(\Omega=(I_N-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_N-\Lambda)\), so distinct source embeddings cannot have the same directed tuple.  Applying \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) therefore yields
\[
 [L:K_G]\leq
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^d A_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.                    \tag{13}
\]
For each \(i\), exactly two selections in the corresponding three factors produce \(A_iC_iZ\); multiplying these independent choices proves the last equality.

Conversely, each formal section constructed above defines a homomorphism from the integral incidence ring to \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\), and all these homomorphisms restrict to the same injective covariance translation.  The image contains \(M_0\) algebraically independent translated covariance coordinates.  By (10) and \(R_{\mathrm{inc}}/I_G\cong R_{\mathrm{src}}\) from \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), the domain also has dimension \(M_0\).  The prime kernel of each section consequently has height zero; since the domain is integral, that kernel is zero.  Passing to fraction fields gives \(2^d\) embeddings of \(L\) over the common embedded copy of \(K_G\).  Their restrictions to \(K_G(z_1)\) are distinct because their \(z_1\)-series have pairwise distinct constant terms.  It follows that
\[
 2^d\leq[K_G(z_1):K_G]\leq[L:K_G]\leq2^d.                   \tag{14}
\]
Thus
\[
 d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,N})=2^d=2^{k+1}.                 \tag{15}
\]
Characteristic zero makes the minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) separable.  After clearing its coefficient denominators, exclude the zero sets of those denominators and of its nonzero discriminant.  This is a proper algebraic exceptional set, and on its nonempty Zariski-open complement the \(2^d\) roots are distinct.  The affine-coordinate conclusion of \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) identifies those roots with exactly the finite queried-coordinate projection.

For \(n>N\), append a new vertex \(w\) that is bidirected with every old vertex, add the directed edge \(0\to w\), and put that edge in \(T\).  No missing residual then involves \(w\).  Let \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\), let \(s_w\) denote the new covariance row, and write \(L_0,K_0\) and \(L_1,K_1\) for the source and covariance fields before and after this extension.  Conditional on the old source coordinates and \(x_w\), covariance congruence is an invertible triangular polynomial change between the allowed new disturbance row and \(s_w\).  Therefore
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,s_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(s_w),                        \tag{16}
\]
where \(x_w\) and the entries of \(s_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0\).  The minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) over \(K_0\) remains irreducible over the purely transcendental extension \(K_0(s_w)\): indeed, a factorization over the latter field can be cleared of denominators and common polynomial content; degrees in the indeterminates \(s_w\) add in the resulting polynomial domain, whereas the original polynomial has degree zero in them, so the factors already lie in \(K_0[t]\).  Consequently
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.                          \tag{17}
\]
Iteration proves (15) for every \(n\geq2k+4\).  Each added edge is a tree edge, so (2) and the excess budget remain valid.  Finally, \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) gives \(D_k(n)\leq2^{k+1}\), while the constructed query gives the reverse inequality.  Hence
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\geq2k+4),
\]
and the discriminant argument above gives the claimed nonempty Zariski-open set on which the original queried coefficient separates all algebraic branches.
body.justification: A uniform attaining region turns the exponent from a loose Bezout count into a sharp coordinate frontier for a substantial size range.
body.gap: Foygel, Draisma, and Drton already exhibit cubic and quartic behavior in small SEMs, but not an all-\(k\) family with one edge separating \(2^{k+1}\) generic branches.
body.consumer: Software maintainers obtain adversarial benchmark families and users obtain a worst-case ambiguity warning indexed by the number of added parents.
